title: What Real Calls Look Like
summary: Patterns from 3,263 recorded calls: where they are won, where they are lost, and the five gaps that show up most.

lessons.title: Won and lost, side by side

blocks.html: Everything in this module comes from 3,263 recorded calls — 1,196 that transferred and 2,067 that didn't. Unusually, we can show you both.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hi, am I speaking with Robert? This is Dana with America's Health on a recorded line, I'm calling about the Medicaid meal service, I just need to confirm you're still receiving Medicaid —

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay, no problem. Have a good day.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hi, am I speaking with Robert? This is Dana with America's Health on a recorded line, calling about the Medicaid meal service. I just need to confirm you're still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: I understand, but groceries are NOT getting any cheaper. You are ALREADY approved for up to three meals at NO cost and this is INCLUDED in your Medicaid. I just need to confirm — you are still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (continues to borough, ZIP, double confirm, transfer)

blocks.html: Same objection, same opening. The difference is one sentence and no pause.

blocks.question: What separates the two calls above?
choices: The opening was better in the second
The agent rebutted immediately instead of accepting the no

blocks.title: Four of the five are the same habit
blocks.html: Asking and not waiting. The question gets said, the agent keeps talking, and nothing is actually verified. The dialer records it as asked.
The fix isn't more words. It's stopping after each question until you hear an answer.

blocks.question: An agent asks about Medicaid and immediately continues into the borough question. How does that score?
choices: Asked but not waited — nothing was verified

blocks.html:
Of the 2,067 lost calls, the loss almost always happens in one of three places:

  1. The first five seconds — consumer disengages during the identity check, before they know what the call is
  2. The first brush-off — “not interested”, “I don't need it”, “I'm busy”, unrebutted
  3. The confusion point — stacked questions with no pauses, and the consumer never understands what is being offered

blocks.title: The third one is self-inflicted
blocks.html: One real loss was summarised as: “stacked questions with no pauses; consumer never understood the offer and declined.” Slowing down is not the opposite of speed — pausing after a question is what keeps the call alive.
Say what the call is about early. A consumer who knows free meals are on the table behaves differently from one who thinks they're being sold something.

blocks.question: Where is the single most common place a call is lost?
blocks.explanation: And more than half of those got no rebuttal at all.

blocks.html: About one call in five on this campaign comes in rather than goes out. The consumer rang you.

Everything else is identical: all nine steps, the Medicaid question, the borough, the ZIP, the double confirm, permission, handoff. What changes is only the opening — don't tell someone who just called you that you're giving them a quick call.

blocks.question: On an inbound call, which steps can you skip?

lessons.title: What the best agents do differently

blocks.html:
Across the top performers' calls, three habits stand out, and none of them are clever:

  • They say what the call is about in the first sentence
  • They never let a brush-off sit — the rebuttal lands immediately
  • They stop talking after each question

blocks.title: That's it
blocks.html: No special lines, no tricks. The approved script, delivered without pauses in the wrong places and with pauses in the right ones.

blocks.question: What do the top performers have in common?
choices: They rebut immediately and wait after each question
They skip the ZIP to save time
